title: Multi-Digit Multiplication and Division
bigQuestion: How can breaking a big multiplication or division into smaller pieces give an exact answer you can trust?

story.title: Too Many Desks to Count
story.kicker: A custodian needs one number for the whole school, and counting desks one by one would take all day.
paragraphs: Mr. Alvarez keeps the desks working at Lincoln Elementary. Every desk has a chair. Every chair has four rubber feet. The feet wear out, and the district wants to know how many to order. His first job is simple to say and hard to do: count every desk in the school. The school has 27 classrooms. Each classroom has 34 desks.

Mr. Alvarez could walk into every room and count. That is 27 rooms, 34 desks each, and one long afternoon. A fourth grader named Dee was eating lunch nearby. She said, "You do not need to count them. You need to multiply." Mr. Alvarez knew his times tables. But 27 × 34 is not on any times table.

Dee drew a rectangle on a napkin. She cut it into four pieces. "Twenty times thirty is 600," she said. "Twenty times four is 80. Seven times thirty is 210. Seven times four is 28." She added the four pieces: 600 + 80 + 210 + 28 = 918. There were 918 desks in the school, and she never left the lunch table.

Mr. Alvarez checked it a different way. He rounded: 30 rooms times 30 desks is 900. The answer 918 was close to 900, so it made sense. Then he had a new question. There were 918 chairs with four feet each, and the feet came in boxes of 50. How many boxes should he order? That question needs multiplication and division, and a plan for what to do with the leftovers.
story.think: Dee split 27 × 34 into four smaller multiplications she could do in her head. Why does adding those four pieces give the same answer as 27 × 34?

lessons.title: Multiplying by Tens and Hundreds
lessons.mainIdea: To multiply by a multiple of ten or a hundred, multiply the basic fact, then attach the zeros.
reading: A pack of gum has 6 pieces. A box holds 40 packs. How many pieces are in a box? Think of 40 as 4 tens. Then 6 × 40 is 6 × 4 tens, which is 24 tens. Twenty-four tens is 240. So a box holds 240 pieces. Every number that ends in zero is a *multiple of ten*, and this trick works for all of them. Multiply the front digits, then count the zeros back on.

Try 30 × 70. The basic fact is 3 × 7 = 21. The two *factors* have one zero each, so the *product* gets two zeros: 2,100. Try 8 × 600. The basic fact is 8 × 6 = 48. There are two zeros, so the product is 4,800. Try 50 × 400. The fact is 5 × 4 = 20, and there are three zeros to attach, so the product is 20,000. Say it as "20 thousand" to hear why.

A common mistake happens when the basic fact itself ends in zero. For 50 × 40, a student finds 5 × 4 = 20 and writes 200. But 200 has only one zero attached to 20. The factors have two zeros, so the answer must be 2,000. Write the basic fact first, then draw one zero for each zero in the factors. Zeros from the fact and zeros from the factors both stay.

words.d: a number you get by multiplying a whole number by 10, such as 30, 40, or 700
a number being multiplied; in 30 × 70, both 30 and 70 are factors
the answer to a multiplication problem; 30 × 70 = 2,100, so 2,100 is the product

look.title: Multiplying 7 by Powers of Ten
look.cite: pattern table for this lesson, computed from the products shown
look.prompt: What happens to the product each time you add a zero to the second factor? Use the pattern to find 7 × 100,000 and 70 × 1,000.

check.q: What is 40 × 90?
check.why: 4 × 9 = 36, and the factors have two zeros, so the product is 3,600.

check.q: What is 7 × 500?
check.why: 7 × 5 = 35, then attach the two zeros from 500. The product is 3,500.

check.q: Which number is equal to 30 × 800?
check.why: 3 × 8 = 24, and the factors have three zeros in all. The product is 24,000.

lessons.title: The Area Model
lessons.mainIdea: Split each factor by place value, multiply every part by every other part, and add the pieces.
reading: A garden is 23 feet long and 14 feet wide. Its area is 23 × 14 square feet. Draw the garden as a rectangle. Cut the long side into 20 and 3. Cut the short side into 10 and 4. Now the garden is four smaller rectangles. This drawing is an *area model*. Each small rectangle has an area you can find with a basic fact and some zeros.

Find the four pieces. The 20 by 10 piece is 200. The 20 by 4 piece is 80. The 3 by 10 piece is 30. The 3 by 4 piece is 12. Add them: 200 + 80 + 30 + 12 = 322. So 23 × 14 = 322 square feet. Check another way: 23 × 10 = 230 and 23 × 4 = 92, and 230 + 92 = 322. When you *decompose* the factors this way, nothing is lost.

The most common mistake is to multiply only the matching parts: 20 × 10 = 200 and 3 × 4 = 12, giving 212. That skips two whole pieces of the garden. Every part of one factor must meet every part of the other. Two parts times two parts always makes four pieces. Draw the rectangle and label every piece before you add. If a piece is missing, the drawing will show a hole.

words.d: a rectangle cut into pieces to show a multiplication, where each piece is a smaller product
to break a number into parts by place value, like 23 into 20 + 3

look.title: A Bigger Garden
look.text: A garden is 36 feet by 25 feet. Draw a rectangle. Cut 36 into 30 and 6. Cut 25 into 20 and 5. Label the four pieces: 30 × 20, 30 × 5, 6 × 20, and 6 × 5. Find each piece, then add all four.
look.prompt: What is the area of the garden? Which piece was the biggest, and which was the smallest?

check.q: The area model for 42 × 17 has pieces 40 × 10, 40 × 7, 2 × 10, and 2 × 7. What is the product?
A student finds 23 × 14 using pieces 20 × 10, 20 × 4, and 3 × 4. Which piece is missing?
check.why: The 3 from 23 must also meet the 10 from 14. The missing piece is 3 × 10 = 30.

check.q: Use an area model to find 58 × 31.

lessons.title: Partial Products
lessons.mainIdea: Partial products are the pieces of an area model written in a column, then added.
reading: A theater has 46 rows with 27 seats in each row. To find 46 × 27 without a drawing, write the pieces in a column. Each piece is a *partial product*, part of the whole answer. Ones times ones: 6 × 7 = 42. Tens times ones: 40 × 7 = 280. Ones times tens: 6 × 20 = 120. Tens times tens: 40 × 20 = 800. These are the same four pieces the area model gives.

Now add the partial products: 42 + 280 + 120 + 800 = 1,242. The theater has 1,242 seats. Check with a different route: 46 × 20 = 920 and 46 × 7 = 322, and 920 + 322 = 1,242. The method also works for three-digit numbers. For 213 × 4, the partial products are 3 × 4 = 12, 10 × 4 = 40, and 200 × 4 = 800. The *sum* is 852.

The most common mistake is forgetting the zeros on a partial product. A student writes 4 × 2 = 8 instead of 4 × 200 = 800, and the answer comes out about 800 too small. Say the full value of each digit before multiplying: "two hundred times four." Another mistake is skipping a piece. For a two-digit times two-digit problem, count your partial products. There must be four.

words.d: one piece of a multiplication, such as 40 × 7 = 280 when finding 46 × 27
the total when you add; the partial products are added to get the full product

look.title: Eight Boxes of Tiles
look.text: A box holds 125 tiles. A contractor buys 8 boxes. Write the partial products for 125 × 8. Start with the ones: 5 × 8. Then the tens: 20 × 8. Then the hundreds: 100 × 8. Add the three pieces.
look.prompt: How many tiles did the contractor buy? Why are there only three partial products instead of four?

check.q: What is the sum of the partial products for 34 × 12?
What is 307 × 6?
check.why: 7 × 6 = 42, 0 × 6 = 0, 300 × 6 = 1,800. The sum is 1,842. Writing 30 × 6 instead of 300 × 6 gives the wrong answer 222.

check.q: A student writes these partial products for 52 × 43. Which one is wrong?
check.why: 5 × 4 = 20, and the factors have two zeros, so 50 × 40 = 2,000, not 200.

lessons.title: The Standard Algorithm
lessons.mainIdea: The standard algorithm multiplies by the ones digit, then by the tens digit with a placeholder zero, and adds the two lines.
reading: Back to the 27 classrooms with 34 desks each. The *standard algorithm* is a short way to write the partial products. Write 27 on top and 34 below it. First multiply 27 by the ones digit, 4. Since 7 × 4 = 28, write 8 and regroup 2. Then 2 × 4 = 8, plus the 2 is 10. The first line is 108. That line is 27 × 4.

Now multiply 27 by the tens digit, 3. But the 3 stands for 30, so first write a *placeholder zero* in the ones place of the second line. Then 7 × 3 = 21, write 1, regroup 2. Next 2 × 3 = 6, plus 2 is 8. The second line is 810, which is 27 × 30. Add the lines: 108 + 810 = 918. The four partial products 28, 80, 210, and 600 are all hidden inside those two lines.

The most common mistake is skipping the placeholder zero. Then the second line reads 81 instead of 810, and the sum is 189 instead of 918. An estimate catches it: 30 × 30 = 900, and 189 is nowhere near 900. The method works for larger numbers too. For 146 × 23, the lines are 146 × 3 = 438 and 146 × 20 = 2,920, and 438 + 2,920 = 3,358.

words.d: the usual step-by-step written method for multiplying, with one line for each digit of the second factor
the 0 written at the end of the second line to show you are multiplying by tens, not ones

look.title: Rows of Seats
look.text: A gym has 38 rows of bleachers with 46 seats in each row. Use the standard algorithm. First line: 38 × 6. Second line: write a placeholder zero, then 38 × 4. Add the two lines. Before you start, estimate with 40 × 50.
look.prompt: How many seats are in the gym? Is your answer close to the estimate?

check.q: What is 27 × 34?
What is 64 × 29?
When multiplying 27 × 34, why do you write a 0 at the end of the second line?
choices: Because every second line ends in zero for neatness
Because 27 has no zeros in it
Because the 3 in 34 means 30, so the line is 27 × 30
Because you are adding 10 to the answer
check.why: The 3 is in the tens place and stands for 30. Multiplying by 30 gives a number ending in 0.

lessons.title: Partial Quotients
lessons.mainIdea: Divide by taking away easy groups of the divisor, then add up how many groups you took.
reading: A shop packs 372 muffins into boxes of 12. How many boxes? This is 372 ÷ 12. The number being divided, 372, is the *dividend*. The number you divide by, 12, is the *divisor*. The answer is the *quotient*. Instead of finding it all at once, take away easy groups. Ten boxes hold 120 muffins. Take 120 from 372, leaving 252. Ten more boxes: 252 − 120 = 132. Ten more: 132 − 120 = 12.

Now only 12 muffins are left, which is exactly one more box. The groups you took were 10, 10, 10, and 1. Each of those is a *partial quotient*. Add them: 10 + 10 + 10 + 1 = 31 boxes. Check: 12 × 31 = 372. With one-digit divisors you can take bigger groups. For 856 ÷ 4, take 200 groups (800), leaving 56. Take 10 groups (40), leaving 16. Take 4 groups (16), leaving 0. The quotient is 200 + 10 + 4 = 214.

The most common mistake is forgetting to add the partial quotients at the end. A student stops at the last group and writes 4 instead of 214. Keep a column on the side and add it when the leftover is smaller than the divisor. Another mistake is a subtraction slip in the middle. Check each subtraction before moving on. There is no single right way to choose groups. Bigger groups mean fewer steps.

words.d: the number being divided; in 372 ÷ 12, the dividend is 372
the number you divide by; in 372 ÷ 12, the divisor is 12
the answer to a division problem; 372 ÷ 12 = 31, so 31 is the quotient
one easy group taken away during division, like taking 10 groups of 12 from 372

look.title: Sharing 645 Stickers
look.text: A teacher has 645 stickers to split evenly among 5 classes. Start with a big group: 100 stickers per class uses 500, leaving 145. Then 20 per class uses 100, leaving 45. Then 9 per class uses 45, leaving 0. Add the partial quotients.
look.prompt: How many stickers does each class get? Check your answer by multiplying it by 5.

check.q: What is 924 ÷ 4?
check.why: 200 groups use 800, leaving 124. 30 groups use 120, leaving 4. 1 more group. 200 + 30 + 1 = 231. Check: 4 × 231 = 924.

check.q: A student divides 429 ÷ 13 using partial quotients of 20, 10, and 3. What is the quotient?
check.why: Add the partial quotients: 20 + 10 + 3 = 33. Check: 13 × 33 = 429.

check.q: What is 1,368 ÷ 6?
check.why: 200 groups use 1,200, leaving 168. 20 groups use 120, leaving 48. 8 groups use 48. The quotient is 200 + 20 + 8 = 228.

lessons.title: Long Division
lessons.mainIdea: Long division works one place at a time from the left: divide, multiply, subtract, bring down, repeat.
reading: A charity splits 2,596 cans of food evenly among 4 food pantries. *Long division* finds 2,596 ÷ 4 one place at a time. Start at the left. Does 4 go into 2? No. Into 25? Yes, 6 times, since 4 × 6 = 24. Write 6 above the 5. Subtract: 25 − 24 = 1. *Bring down* the 9 to make 19. Then 4 goes into 19 four times, since 4 × 4 = 16. Write 4. Subtract: 19 − 16 = 3.

Bring down the 6 to make 36. Then 4 goes into 36 nine times, since 4 × 9 = 36. Write 9. Subtract: 36 − 36 = 0. The quotient is 649 cans per pantry. Check: 4 × 649 = 2,596. Two-digit divisors follow the same steps. For 1,505 ÷ 35, does 35 go into 150? Yes, 4 times, 4 × 35 = 140, and 150 − 140 = 10. Bring down 5 to make 105. Then 35 goes into 105 three times. The quotient is 43.

The most common mistake is losing a zero in the quotient. For 3,015 ÷ 3, the steps are 3 into 3 once, 3 into 0 zero times, 3 into 1 zero times, then 3 into 15 five times. The quotient is 1,005. A student who skips the zeros writes 15 or 105. Every time you bring down a digit, you must write a digit in the quotient, even when that digit is 0. Estimate first: 3,000 ÷ 3 = 1,000, so 15 cannot be right.

words.d: a written method that divides one place at a time, repeating divide, multiply, subtract, and bring down
to copy the next digit of the dividend beside the leftover so you can keep dividing

look.title: A Week of Newspapers
look.text: A printer makes 3,612 copies of a school paper over 7 days, the same number each day. Use long division to find 3,612 ÷ 7. Start with 36: 7 goes in 5 times with 1 left. Bring down the 1 to make 11. Keep going until you bring down the 2.
look.prompt: How many copies were printed each day? Multiply your quotient by 7 to check.

check.q: What is 2,596 ÷ 4?
check.why: 4 into 25 is 6 with 1 left; 4 into 19 is 4 with 3 left; 4 into 36 is 9. The quotient is 649, and 4 × 649 = 2,596.

check.q: What is 4,020 ÷ 5?
check.why: 5 into 40 is 8 with 0 left; 5 into 2 is 0, so write a 0; 5 into 20 is 4. The quotient is 804. Check: 5 × 804 = 4,020.

check.q: What is 1,932 ÷ 42?
check.why: 42 into 193 is 4, since 42 × 4 = 168, leaving 25. Bring down 2 to make 252, and 42 × 6 = 252. The quotient is 46.

lessons.title: What the Remainder Means
lessons.mainIdea: A remainder is what is left after dividing, and the situation tells you whether to round up, drop it, or report it.
reading: A school sends 125 students on a trip. Each bus holds 40. Divide: 125 ÷ 40 = 3 with 5 left over. The 5 is the *remainder*, the part that does not fill a whole group. Write it as 3 R 5. But "3 R 5 buses" is not an answer. Three buses leave 5 students at school. The school needs 4 buses. When everyone or everything must fit, round the quotient up.

The same division can mean different things. Suppose 125 cookies are shared by 40 kids. Each kid gets 3 cookies, and 5 cookies are left on the tray. Here the remainder is the answer to "how many are left?" Now suppose you have $125 and tickets cost $40. You can buy 3 tickets. The $5 left is not enough for another, so drop the remainder. To *interpret* the remainder means deciding which of these fits the story.

Ask three questions. Does everything have to fit? Then round the quotient up. Is the question about the leftover? Then the remainder is the answer. Can you only count whole items? Then drop the remainder. The common mistake is writing "3 R 5" and stopping. A remainder is never the final answer to a word problem. Read the last sentence of the problem again and decide what the leftover means.

words.d: the amount left over after dividing into equal groups; 125 ÷ 40 = 3 with a remainder of 5
to decide what a number means in a real situation, such as whether a remainder means one more bus

look.title: Chairs in Rows
look.text: A custodian sets up 250 chairs for a concert in rows of 12. Divide 250 ÷ 12. Twenty rows use 240 chairs, and 10 chairs are left. Now think about three different questions. How many full rows are there? How many chairs are in the short row at the back? How many rows are there in all, if every chair must be in a row?
look.prompt: Give all three answers. Which question used the remainder, which dropped it, and which rounded up?

check.q: A photo album holds 8 photos per page. How many pages are needed for 94 photos?
check.why: 94 ÷ 8 = 11 with 6 left over. Those 6 photos need one more page, so 12 pages.

check.q: Notebooks cost $6 each. How many can you buy with $50?
check.why: 50 ÷ 6 = 8 with $2 left over. Two dollars cannot buy another notebook, so the answer is 8.

check.q: 200 marbles are shared equally among 7 friends. How many marbles are left over?
check.why: 7 × 28 = 196, and 200 − 196 = 4. Each friend gets 28, and 4 marbles are left.

lessons.title: Estimating Products and Quotients
lessons.mainIdea: Round the factors, or pick compatible numbers, to get a quick estimate before you compute.
reading: A theater sells 48 tickets for each of 23 shows. About how many tickets is that? To *estimate*, round each factor. 48 is close to 50, and 23 is close to 20. Then 50 × 20 = 1,000. The exact product is 48 × 23 = 1,104, so the estimate is close. Rounding one factor up and the other down often keeps the estimate near the real answer.

For division, rounding is not always enough. Take 1,789 ÷ 6. Rounding gives 1,800 ÷ 6, and 18 ÷ 6 = 3 is a basic fact, so the estimate is 300. Numbers that make a basic fact together, like 1,800 and 6, are called *compatible numbers*. For 4,182 ÷ 7, choose 4,200, since 42 ÷ 7 = 6. The estimate is 600. The exact quotient, 597 R 3, is very close.

A common mistake is rounding both factors up. For 48 × 23, rounding to 50 × 30 gives 1,500, which is almost 400 too high. Another mistake is choosing a rounded dividend that does not match the divisor, like 1,800 ÷ 7. Look for a number the divisor goes into evenly. Always write your estimate down before you compute. Then compare the two. If they are far apart, look for the error.

words.d: a quick, close answer found by rounding or using easier numbers
numbers that are easy to compute together, like 4,200 and 7, because 42 ÷ 7 is a basic fact

look.title: A Month of Movies
look.text: A movie theater sells about 312 tickets every day. The manager wants a quick idea of the tickets sold in 28 days. Round 312 to the nearest hundred and 28 to the nearest ten, then multiply. Then find the exact product with partial products or the standard algorithm.
look.prompt: What is the estimate, and what is the exact product? Was the estimate too high or too low, and why?

check.q: Which is the best estimate for 61 × 39?
check.why: Round to 60 × 40 = 2,400. The exact product is 2,379, so the estimate is close.

check.q: Estimate 3,610 ÷ 9 using compatible numbers.
check.why: 3,600 is compatible with 9 because 36 ÷ 9 = 4. So 3,600 ÷ 9 = 400.

check.q: Which estimate is closest to 297 × 4?
check.why: 297 rounds to 300, and 300 × 4 = 1,200. The exact product is 1,188.

lessons.title: Multi-Step Problems
lessons.mainIdea: Break a multi-step problem into a plan, do one step at a time, and check that the last step answers the question.
reading: A field trip uses 4 buses that each hold 48 people. There are 175 students and 12 adults going. How many seats will be empty? This is a *multi-step problem*. No single operation answers it. First make a *plan*. Step 1: find the seats, 4 × 48. Step 2: find the people, 175 + 12. Step 3: subtract the people from the seats.

Now do the steps. Step 1: 4 × 48 = 192 seats. Step 2: 175 + 12 = 187 people. Step 3: 192 − 187 = 5 empty seats. Read the question again: "How many seats will be empty?" The answer is 5 seats. Here is another. A school has 918 desks and gets 96 more. The desks are shared evenly among 26 classrooms. First 918 + 96 = 1,014. Then 1,014 ÷ 26 = 39 desks per room.

The most common mistake is stopping too soon. A student finds 192 seats and writes it down as the answer. But 192 is not what the question asked. Another mistake is doing the steps in the wrong order, like subtracting 12 from 192 before adding the students. Write the plan first, number each step, and put a box around the final answer. Then check that the boxed number answers the actual question.

words.d: a word problem that needs two or more operations to answer
a numbered list of the steps you will do before you start computing

look.title: The Bake Sale
look.text: A class bakes 15 trays of cookies with 24 cookies on each tray. They put the cookies in bags of 6 and sell each bag for $2. Plan the steps: total cookies, then number of bags, then money earned. Do each step and write the answer next to it.
look.prompt: How much money does the class earn if every bag sells? Which step was multiplication, which was division, and which was multiplication again?

check.q: A store buys 24 boxes of pencils with 36 pencils in each box, then repacks them in packs of 8. How many packs?
check.why: 24 × 36 = 864 pencils. Then 864 ÷ 8 = 108 packs.

check.q: Four buses hold 48 people each. 175 students and 12 adults ride. How many seats are empty?
check.why: 4 × 48 = 192 seats, and 175 + 12 = 187 people. Then 192 − 187 = 5 empty seats.

check.q: Ms. Lee buys 6 packs of 12 markers and gives 3 markers to each of her 20 students. How many markers are left?
check.why: 6 × 12 = 72 markers. She gives away 3 × 20 = 60. Then 72 − 60 = 12 markers are left.

lessons.title: Multiply to Check Division
lessons.mainIdea: Multiplication undoes division, so multiply the quotient by the divisor and add any remainder to check.
reading: Earlier we found 1,505 ÷ 35 = 43. Is it right? Multiplication is the *inverse operation* of division, so it can undo the division. Multiply 35 × 43. Using the standard algorithm: 35 × 3 = 105, and 35 × 40 = 1,400. Add: 105 + 1,400 = 1,505. That is the dividend we started with, so the quotient is right. If the product had been anything else, the division had an error somewhere.

When there is a remainder, add it after multiplying. Earlier we found 200 ÷ 7 = 28 R 4. Check: 7 × 28 = 196, then 196 + 4 = 200. Good. The remainder also has a rule of its own. It must always be smaller than the divisor. Suppose a student writes 200 ÷ 7 = 27 R 11. The check works, since 7 × 27 = 189 and 189 + 11 = 200. But 11 is bigger than 7, so one more group of 7 fits. The correct answer is 28 R 4.

Division can check multiplication too. If you found 24 × 7 = 168, then 168 ÷ 7 should be 24, and it is. The most common mistake is checking with the wrong operation, like adding the divisor to the quotient. Adding will never undo dividing. Use the operation that goes the other way, and make sure the answer you get is *reasonable* by comparing it to an estimate.

words.d: an operation that undoes another; multiplication undoes division, and division undoes multiplication
close to an estimate, so it makes sense; an answer far from the estimate needs another look

look.title: Units of Time
look.cite: standard time units; the year is counted as 365 days
look.prompt: Check that 24 × 7 = 168 by dividing 168 ÷ 7. Then check that 1,440 × 7 = 10,080 by dividing 10,080 ÷ 7. Which check was harder, and why?

check.q: Which equation checks that 2,952 ÷ 8 = 369 is correct?
check.why: Multiply the quotient by the divisor. 8 × 369 = 2,400 + 552 = 2,952, the dividend, so the division is right.

check.q: A student says 150 ÷ 6 = 24 R 6. What is wrong?
choices: The remainder cannot equal the divisor, so one more group fits and the answer is 25
The remainder should be 0 and the quotient should stay 24
check.why: A remainder of 6 with a divisor of 6 means one more group of 6 fits. 6 × 25 = 150, so the answer is 25 with no remainder.

check.q: Using the table, which division checks that 24 × 7 = 168?
check.why: Division undoes multiplication. 168 ÷ 7 = 24 gives back the first factor, so the product is right.

review.why: 6 × 7 = 42, and the factors have three zeros in all. The product is 42,000.
8 into 34 is 4 with 2 left; 8 into 25 is 3 with 1 left; 8 into 16 is 2. The quotient is 432. Check: 8 × 432 = 3,456.

review.q: A warehouse packs 1,000 cans into cases of 24. How many full cases can it pack?
review.why: 24 × 41 = 984, and 1,000 − 984 = 16. The 16 leftover cans do not fill a case, so 41 full cases.

review.q: Which is the best estimate for 78 × 52?
review.why: Round to 80 × 50 = 4,000. The exact product is 4,056.

review.q: 213 students are going on a trip. Each bus holds 45. How many buses are needed?
review.why: 213 ÷ 45 = 4 with 33 left over. Those 33 students need another bus, so 5 buses.

review.q: A coach buys 12 packs of 25 trading cards and gives 8 cards to each of 30 players. How many cards are left?
review.why: 12 × 25 = 300 cards. The players get 8 × 30 = 240. Then 300 − 240 = 60 cards are left.
